issues.legal_issue: A dependant has no independent right to compassionate appointment beyond any entitlement conferred by the employer’s scheme or instructions.
material_facts: A deceased bank employee’s family sought compassionate appointment for his son.
The bank had a scheme governing compassionate appointments, and the claim was considered under that scheme.
issues.conclusion: Any claim to compassionate appointment was traceable only to the employer’s scheme or instructions; there was no right to appointment on any other ground.
issues.legal_principle: Article 16(1) guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment, and compassionate appointment is a narrow exception to the general requirement of open, merit-based recruitment. Under Umesh Kumar Nagpal v. State of Haryana (1994) 4 SCC 138, the exception aims to help a family facing sudden crisis and penury, not to grant a post to a deceased employee’s relative. Union Bank of India v. M.T. Latheesh (2006) 7 SCC 350 cautions that indiscriminate compassionate appointments would restrict employment opportunities for others. An entitlement exists only to the extent provided by the employer’s scheme, instructions, or rules.

predicates.compassionate_appointment_claim: A dependant seeks employment because an employee died while in service.
predicates.employer_has_compassionate_appointment_s: The employer has established a scheme governing compassionate appointments.

issues.definition: When a dependant seeks compassionate appointment and the employer has a scheme for it, the claim is limited to what that scheme provides.

issues.legal_issue: An employer may assess eligibility for compassionate appointment by considering the financial resources and circumstances identified in its scheme.
material_facts: The bank’s scheme identified family pension, terminal benefits, investments, income from other sources, family size, and liabilities as factors in assessing financial condition.
The bank’s competent authority considered terminal benefits and investments, pension, agricultural income and land, the family’s residence, and liabilities.
The authority concluded that the family had not been left in penury or without means of livelihood.
issues.conclusion: The competent authority did not err by taking the family’s terminal benefits, investments, pension, and income from agricultural land into account, because the scheme required or permitted those factors to be considered.
issues.legal_principle: The bank’s scheme made the family’s financial condition an important eligibility criterion and specified that pension, gratuity, provident fund, compensation, insurance proceeds and investments, other income, family members’ income, family size, and liabilities be considered. Eligibility must be assessed according to that scheme; the financial sources it identifies may be taken into account.

predicates.compassionate_eligibility_assessment: An employer assesses a dependant’s eligibility for compassionate appointment.
predicates.scheme_identifies_financial_factors: The employer’s scheme identifies financial resources or circumstances as factors in assessing eligibility.
predicates.authority_considers_identified_family_re: The deciding authority considers family resources or circumstances identified by the scheme.

issues.definition: If an eligibility assessment is governed by a scheme that identifies financial factors and the authority considers those factors, the identified family resources may be counted in the assessment.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court may not replace the scheme’s penury criterion with its own assessment of what income is sufficient for a family’s survival.
material_facts: The bank’s competent authority assessed the family’s financial circumstances under the scheme and found that the family was not in penury or without means of livelihood.
The respondent did not contend that the authority’s order was inconsistent with the scheme.
The High Court assessed the family’s monthly income as insufficient to take it out of penury and directed the bank to reconsider the claim.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have substituted its assessment of the family’s financial sufficiency for the competent authority’s decision or diluted the scheme’s penury criterion; its order was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial review of a rejection of compassionate appointment is directed to whether the decision-making process is vitiated or the order is inconsistent with the scheme, not to the reviewing court’s own calculation of reasonable family income. Under General Manager (D&PB) v. Kunti Tiwary (2004) 7 SCC 271, a court cannot dilute the criterion of penury to one of being not very well-to-do. Compassionate appointment cannot be granted contrary to the governing scheme.

predicates.review_of_compassionate_rejection: A court reviews an employer’s rejection of a claim for compassionate appointment.
predicates.authority_applied_scheme_to_financial_ci: The employer’s authority assessed the family’s financial circumstances under the governing scheme.
predicates.no_scheme_noncompliance_was_urged: The claimant did not contend that the employer’s decision failed to comply with the governing scheme.
predicates.reviewing_court_substituted_its_own_penu: The reviewing court made its own assessment of whether the family’s income was sufficient to take it out of penury.

issues.definition: When a court reviews a rejection made after the authority applied the scheme, and no failure to comply with the scheme was urged, the court may not replace the scheme’s penury criterion with its own assessment.
